name: go-qfext (Facebook Quotient Filter for Go)
workload: go test -bench lookup benchmark: quotient filter Contains() (unpacked and bit-packed variants) vs a popular Go Bloom filter library
claimed_speedup: Unpacked quotient filter lookup 20.43 ns/op and packed 30.95 ns/op vs Bloom filter 74.47 ns/op (~3.6x and ~2.4x faster respectively; native Go map lookup shown for reference at 9.373 ns/op)
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain default, `go test -run=xxx -bench=.`; no special build flags stated
tradeoffs: Static/quotient-hash structure; bit-packing trades speed for memory; designed for large pre-built models loaded from disk, not a general dynamic set
caveats: Single benchmark run on one laptop, no repeated trials or variance reported; the Bloom filter compared against is a specific third-party Go library (bits-and-blooms/bloom v3), not a canonical C/C++ implementation
found_via: gh search repos "quotient filter" --sort stars -> opened facebookincubator/go-qfext README

name: xorfilter (Go binary fuse / xor filter reference implementation)
workload: Static-set membership filter storage-overhead comparison (binary fuse vs xor vs Bloom filters), evaluated in the companion Journal of Experimental Algorithmics papers
claimed_speedup: Per the binary fuse filter paper (arXiv:2201.01174) abstract: storage within 13% of the information-theoretic lower bound for binary fuse filters vs 23% for xor filters and 44% for Bloom filters; construction "more than twice as fast" as xor filters (derived from paper abstract, not this repo's own README numbers)
stars_or_usage: 764 stars; used in CockroachDB Pebble, Oracle Coherence Go client, MatrixOne
tradeoffs: Immutable/static filter, must rebuild to add keys; construction needs substantially more temporary memory than the final filter size; no deletion support
caveats: This repo's own README shows only a comparison image, no numeric benchmark table; the 13%/23%/44% figures come from the companion peer-reviewed paper's abstract, not independently reproduced against this Go code this session
found_via: Starting query 'fastfilter benchmark results xor binary fuse ribbon' -> gh search repos 'xor filter' -> arXiv abstract for binary fuse paper

name: xorf (Rust xor / binary fuse filter crate)
workload: Same static-set membership storage-overhead comparison as the binary fuse filter paper (xor/binary fuse vs Bloom filters)
claimed_speedup: README states "Xor filters are faster and smaller than Bloom and Cuckoo filters"; per the backing paper (arXiv:2201.01174) binary fuse filters (implemented here) reach storage within 13% of the theoretical lower bound vs 44% for Bloom filters (derived from paper abstract, not this crate's own benchmarks)
tradeoffs: no_std + alloc design; immutable static filter; binary-fuse feature pulls in a `libm` dependency
caveats: No numeric benchmark table found in this crate's own README/docs; comparative numbers are inherited from the general binary fuse filter paper, not measured against this specific Rust implementation this session
found_via: gh search repos 'xor filter' --sort stars -> opened ayazhafiz/xorf README

name: RocksDB Ribbon Filter
workload: RocksDB SST-block filter construction/query cost for point lookups, measured with RocksDB's own filter_bench tool (`./filter_bench -impl=2|3 -quick -m_keys_total_max=200 -use_full_block_reader`)
claimed_speedup: ~30% smaller than a Bloom filter at the same false-positive rate (7 bits/key Ribbon vs 10 bits/key Bloom, RocksDB's typical config), at a cost of ~4.4x construction CPU (140 ns/key vs 32 ns/key) and ~20% slower queries (600 ns/key vs 500 ns/key); numbers quoted verbatim from the RocksDB engineering blog post
stars_or_usage: 32.1k stars; Ribbon filter shipped in production RocksDB since v6.15
tradeoffs: Higher construction CPU and ~3x more temporary memory during build (~230 bits/key vs ~75 for Bloom); relatively worse (more CPU) at low false-positive rates; RocksDB recommends Ribbon only for filters kept in memory beyond roughly an hour
caveats: CPU model/hardware not stated in the blog post, and the numbers come from RocksDB's own first-party filter_bench tool with only partial methodology disclosed, capping tier at C per the hard rules. A peer-reviewed backing paper (arXiv:2103.02515, appeared at ESA 2021) independently states Ribbon filters reach <10% space overhead vs the information-theoretic bound, versus >=20% for prior filters generally -- opened and confirmed, but that abstract text does not explicitly name "Bloom filter" in the exact sentence extracted.
found_via: HN Algolia 'ribbon filter' -> rocksdb.org blog post; corroborated via gh api code search 'ribbon filter' in facebook/rocksdb

name: Cuckoo Filter (original C++ reference implementation)
workload: General approximate set-membership queries; no numeric benchmark table found in the repo README itself this session
claimed_speedup: README states the cuckoo filter "could use less space than conventional Bloom filters, for applications that require low false positive rates (< 3%)"; the underlying paper is titled "Cuckoo Filter: Practically Better Than Bloom" (CoNEXT 2014). No numeric figures were verified from an opened page this session.
stars_or_usage: 1,013 stars; the canonical reference implementation cited by nearly every cuckoo filter port and by the FastFilter benchmark suite's credits
tradeoffs: No OSI-approved license on the repo (license field is NOASSERTION), so the code can be studied but not safely reused verbatim; unmaintained since 2021
caveats: Tier D: only a qualitative claim ("better than Bloom", low space at FPR<3%) with no numbers on any page opened this session; included under the D-tier notability exception (>1k stars), limited to one such entry per this run
found_via: gh search repos 'cuckoo filter' --sort stars; corroborated by HN Algolia 'cuckoo filter' (100-pt Show HN linking to the original CMU PDF)

name: Counting Quotient Filter (CQF)
baseline: counting Bloom filter (and Bloom filter generally)
workload: In-memory and SSD-resident insert/query throughput for approximate membership + counting, per the SIGMOD 2017 paper "A General-Purpose Counting Filter: Making Every Bit Count"
claimed_speedup: "In-memory inserts and queries up to an order-of-magnitude faster than the original [quotient] filter, several times faster than a Bloom filter"; on SSD, CQF "outperforms all structures by a factor of at least 2" due to better data locality (as quoted by the independent paper-summary blog blog.acolyer.org, "the morning paper")
stars_or_usage: 132 stars; used as a component in several genomics/bioinformatics k-mer counting tools
tradeoffs: Fastest path needs Haswell+ select instructions (has a slower fallback for older CPUs); depends on libssl; smaller ecosystem/tooling than Bloom filters
caveats: Exact figures (order-of-magnitude, several-times, 2x) are quoted from an independent third-party paper summary, not directly extracted from the paywalled ACM DL paper itself -- two direct fetch attempts (dl.acm.org and the author's PDF) both failed with 403 this session
found_via: HN Algolia 'quotient filter' -> blog.acolyer.org summary of the SIGMOD 2017 paper

name: cuSBF (GPU Minimizer-Aware Super Bloom Filter)
baseline: Bloom filter (NVIDIA cuCollections GPU Blocked Bloom Filter, GBBF)
workload: Batch k-mer insertion and query throughput on genomic sequence data, Config<31,28,16,4>, on a smaller filter (C. elegans, ~100M k-mers) and a large filter (CHM13, ~3.1B k-mers)
claimed_speedup: 9.1x faster insert / 7.7x faster query vs GPU Blocked Bloom Filter (GBBF/cuCollections) on the ~100M k-mer filter; 8.2x insert / 7.6x query on the ~3.1B k-mer filter (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU); also reported to beat GPU Cuckoo-GPU by 8.0-3427x, GPU Two-Choice Filter by 12-67x, and GPU Counting Quotient Filter (GQF) by 13-69x, and CPU Super Bloom by 59-234x
compiler_and_flags: CUDA Toolkit >=13.1, GCC/Clang host compiler (C++20), Meson/Ninja build, Google Benchmark suite
hardware: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU; CPU baseline (Super Bloom) run on an Intel Xeon w9-3595X with 120 threads
stars_or_usage: 7 stars; brand-new companion code for a 2026 arXiv paper
tradeoffs: GPU-only, requires NVIDIA compute capability 8.0+ and CUDA 13.1+; Linux-only build (uses mmap and GNU statement expressions); specialized for genomic minimizer/k-mer workloads rather than a general-purpose drop-in filter; needs the findere scheme tuned to match GBBF's false-positive rate at low bits/k-mer
caveats: Very new project (7 stars) and paper (arXiv:2606.24417, 2026); benchmark numbers are the project's own first-party results (not yet independently reproduced by a third party), though hardware, compiler, and build tooling are all explicitly stated, which is why it is still rated tier A rather than C. Note one of its comparison baselines, GPU Cuckoo-GPU (tdortman/Cuckoo-GPU), is already in the known-catalogued list, so only the cuSBF-vs-GBBF (Bloom) result is reported as this entry's primary claim.
found_via: arXiv API query 'approximate membership query AND evaluation' -> arXiv:2606.24417 abstract -> gh search code 'cuSBF' -> tdortman/cuSBF README
